meta.basis: General industry practice for institutional and wholesale asset management distribution. Not a disclosed Goldman Sachs process. Who leads at each stage varies by firm, team and client; treat the allocation between sales and relationship management as illustrative.

stages.name: Research and targeting
stages.plain: Working out which organisations might have a need the firm can genuinely meet, before anyone picks up the phone.
stages.what_happens: The team maps a market: who the asset owners are, how large they are, who advises them, which managers they use, when contracts or strategy reviews fall due, and which searches are open. Public documents do most of the work: annual reports, statements of investment principles, committee papers, consultant search notices and trade press. Prospects are ranked by fit and timing, and some are deliberately set aside.
stages.who_leads: Sales, with consultant relations where a consultant controls access.
stages.who_supports: Analysts, marketing and data teams; relationship managers who know related organisations.
junior_produces: One-page prospect briefing with sources and a list of what is not known
Tracker of contract end dates, strategy reviews and open searches
Map of who advises whom (consultant, independent trustee, actuary)
CRM clean-up: correct contacts, roles and meeting history
stages.client_side: Nobody yet. The prospect does not know it is being researched and owes the firm nothing.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client's first conversation is with someone who already understands its structure and constraints and does not waste its time on products that cannot fit.
failure_points: Targeting by size alone and ignoring fit
Out-of-date information presented as current
Pursuing a search where the firm's strategy is not rated by the client's consultant
Treating a public document as telling the whole story
stages.sales_vs_rm: Almost entirely an origination activity. Relationship managers contribute intelligence about clients that share a consultant, sponsor or trustee.
stages.duration_note: Continuous background work; intensity rises when a search is announced.

stages.name: First contact and discovery
stages.plain: The first conversations, where the aim is to understand the client's problem, not to present a product.
stages.what_happens: An introduction is made directly, through a consultant or at an industry event. Early meetings are mostly questions: what the organisation is trying to achieve, what constrains it (liabilities, liquidity needs, governance time, regulation, beliefs), how decisions are made and by whom, and what has disappointed it before. The firm also decides whether it should compete at all.
stages.who_supports: A product or investment specialist if the conversation turns technical; senior sponsor for very large prospects.
junior_produces: Question list tailored to the prospect
Meeting notes written up the same day, separating what was said from what was inferred
Contact map: who decides, who advises, who influences, who operates
Follow-up email draft with the material promised
stages.client_side: Usually an investment officer, pensions manager or chief investment officer; sometimes the consultant alone. They need to know quickly whether this manager is worth further time.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client is asked questions that sharpen its own understanding of the problem, and is told honestly if the firm is not a good fit.
failure_points: Presenting before listening
Speaking only to one contact and mistaking their view for the organisation's
Promising follow-up that does not arrive
Failing to qualify out: continuing because a meeting was friendly
stages.sales_vs_rm: Origination. Where the organisation is already a client for another mandate, the relationship manager normally makes the introduction and may lead.
stages.duration_note: From a single meeting to many months of intermittent contact.

stages.name: Solution design and proposal
stages.plain: Turning what was learned into a specific proposal: which strategy, in what form, on what terms.
stages.what_happens: Sales works with portfolio managers, product specialists and sometimes a solutions team to shape a proposal: the strategy or combination of strategies, the vehicle (pooled fund or segregated mandate), benchmark and guidelines, reporting, indicative fees. Pricing outside the standard schedule needs internal approval. The proposal should state what the approach will not do as clearly as what it will.
stages.who_leads: Sales, with the investment or solutions team owning the investment content.
stages.who_supports: Product specialists, pricing or business management, legal for unusual terms, compliance for review.
junior_produces: First draft of proposal slides from approved content
Data tables: performance, risk and peer comparisons reconciled to official records
Fee illustration on stated assumptions
Version control and compliance-review log
stages.client_side: Investment staff and consultant. They need a proposal that addresses their stated problem and can be compared fairly with others.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client receives a proposal built around its objective and constraints, with trade-offs visible, so it can make an informed comparison.
failure_points: A generic pitch with the client's name on the cover
Fees or terms quoted without approval
Performance shown selectively or for a different vehicle than the one proposed
Over-engineering: a complex solution to a simple need
stages.sales_vs_rm: Origination. For an expansion of an existing mandate the relationship manager often leads because they know the guidelines and history.
stages.duration_note: Days for a standard product; months for a bespoke or multi-asset solution.

stages.name: RFP and due diligence
stages.plain: The formal written stage: answering the client's questionnaire and proving that what was said is true.
stages.what_happens: The client or its consultant issues a request for proposal (RFP) and a due-diligence questionnaire (DDQ) covering organisation, team, process, performance, risk, operations, compliance, responsible investment and fees. Responses are scored. Operational due diligence may include site visits and interviews with risk, compliance and operations staff. For UK occupational schemes appointing a fiduciary manager above the regulatory threshold, a qualifying competitive tender with at least three unconnected providers is required.
stages.who_leads: Sales owns the submission; the RFP team runs the process.
stages.who_supports: Content owners across the firm (portfolio managers, risk, compliance, operations, legal, human resources), each approving the facts in their area.
junior_produces: Question-by-question tracker with owner, status and deadline
First-draft answers from the approved library, updated for the latest quarter
Evidence folder: policies, organisation charts, sample reports
Consistency check between the RFP, the presentation and the factsheet
stages.client_side: Consultant's research and operational due-diligence teams, the client's investment staff, sometimes procurement. They need complete, accurate and comparable answers by the deadline.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client can rely on the answers when it justifies its decision, and discovers no surprises after appointment.
failure_points: Missed deadline or ignored format rules, which can disqualify
Stale library answers (old team names, old assets figures)
Inconsistency between documents
Answering a different question from the one asked
stages.sales_vs_rm: Origination. In a re-tender the relationship manager is deeply involved because the incumbent's record is part of the evidence.
stages.duration_note: Typically weeks, set by the client's timetable.

stages.name: Final presentation and appointment
stages.plain: The shortlist meeting, often called a beauty parade, after which the decision-makers choose.
stages.what_happens: A small number of shortlisted managers present to the decision-making body, such as a trustee board or investment committee, usually for a fixed time with questions. The consultant normally attends and may score. The team presenting is typically the senior salesperson, the portfolio manager and the person who would manage the relationship. The client then decides, sometimes on the day, and informs managers of the outcome.
stages.who_leads: Senior sales with the portfolio manager.
stages.who_supports: The proposed relationship manager, product specialist, team head for large mandates.
junior_produces: Rehearsal pack and timed running order
Bank of likely questions with agreed answers and who takes each
Biographies and leave-behind document
Post-pitch record of every question asked and the outcome, including feedback if lost
stages.client_side: Trustees or committee members, who may be non-specialists with limited time, plus their consultant. They need to understand the proposal, test the people and feel able to defend the choice.
stages.good_execution_changes: The decision-makers understand what they are buying and what could go wrong, and meet the people they will actually deal with.
failure_points: Talking over the audience's level or under it
A portfolio manager who cannot explain simply
Presenting a team the client will never see again
Not asking for feedback after a loss
stages.sales_vs_rm: Origination, but this is where the relationship manager should first appear so the handover is not a surprise.
stages.duration_note: A single meeting; the decision may follow within days or after the next governance meeting.

stages.name: Legal negotiation and onboarding
stages.plain: Agreeing the contract and opening the accounts so the mandate can legally and operationally begin.
stages.what_happens: For a segregated mandate an investment management agreement (IMA) is negotiated: guidelines, benchmark, fees, reporting, liability, termination. For a pooled fund the client completes subscription documents. Client due diligence (know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks) is completed. Custody links, trading accounts and reporting are set up and tested.
stages.who_leads: Onboarding or client implementation team with legal; the relationship manager coordinates the client side.
stages.who_supports: Sales (to honour what was promised), portfolio manager (to confirm guidelines are workable), operations, compliance, tax.
junior_produces: Document checklist and status tracker
Chasing list for outstanding client and custodian items
Comparison of contract terms against the proposal, flagging differences
Reporting set-up specification
stages.client_side: Legal advisers, operations staff, custodian, sometimes the sponsor's treasury. They need a clear list of what is required and prompt answers.
stages.good_execution_changes: The mandate starts on the agreed date with guidelines that say what the client intended.
failure_points: Promises made in the pitch that the contract does not reflect
Guidelines that are ambiguous or cannot be monitored
Slow due-diligence document collection delaying funding
No single owner between sales and relationship management
stages.sales_vs_rm: The seam. In a handover model responsibility passes here; in a paired or single-owner model the same people continue.
stages.duration_note: Weeks to several months, driven by legal negotiation and document collection.

stages.name: Funding and transition
stages.plain: The money or assets actually arrive and the portfolio is built.
stages.what_happens: The client transfers cash or existing securities. If assets come from a previous manager, a transition plan sets out how the old portfolio becomes the new one while controlling cost and market exposure; a specialist transition manager may be used. The portfolio manager invests to the target. Fee accrual starts on funded assets. The first report is produced and checked with unusual care.
stages.who_leads: Operations and the portfolio manager, with the relationship manager as the client's single point of contact.
stages.who_supports: Transition specialists, trading, performance and reporting teams.
junior_produces: Funding timeline with dates and responsible parties
Day-one confirmation to the client of what has been received
Check of the first report against the contract: benchmark, fee basis, guideline tests
Welcome pack: contacts, reporting calendar, escalation route
stages.client_side: Operations and finance staff, custodian, outgoing manager. They need certainty about dates, amounts and who to call.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client's assets are invested as agreed without avoidable cost, and the first report is right.
failure_points: Funding later or smaller than announced
An error in the first report, which sets the tone
Transition costs not explained in advance
Performance inception date disputed
stages.sales_vs_rm: Stewardship begins. An announced mandate is not fee-paying until funded, so sales often stays involved until money arrives.
stages.duration_note: Days for cash into a pooled fund; weeks or longer for a complex transition or phased funding.

stages.name: Ongoing reviews and reporting
stages.plain: The long middle of the relationship: regular reports, review meetings and answering questions.
stages.what_happens: Reports go out on a fixed calendar. Review meetings, typically quarterly to annual, cover performance, positioning, risk, guideline compliance, service and outlook. Between meetings there are ad hoc questions, data requests from the consultant, regulatory reporting needs and operational changes. The relationship manager keeps the internal picture of the client current as people and priorities change.
stages.who_supports: Client service and reporting teams, portfolio managers and product specialists for meetings, consultant relations.
junior_produces: Draft review pack reconciled to the official performance record
Meeting preparation note
Minutes and action log within two working days
Query log with response times
stages.client_side: Investment staff, trustees or committee, consultant, operations and finance. They need accurate information on time and plain explanations.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client understands what it owns and why it has behaved as it has, and can govern the mandate with confidence.
failure_points: Late or wrong reports
Meetings that recite a pack and answer no questions
Actions that are not followed up
Losing touch when the client's staff change
stages.sales_vs_rm: Stewardship. Sales stays informed because a well-served client is the main source of references and further mandates.
stages.duration_note: Years; this stage is most of the relationship.

stages.name: Difficulties
stages.plain: Something goes wrong: performance disappoints, an error occurs, or key people leave.
stages.what_happens: Common triggers are sustained underperformance, a guideline breach or operational error, the departure of a portfolio manager, a change in the firm's ownership or strategy, or a change on the client's side such as a new consultant. The relationship manager establishes facts, informs the client early, brings the right senior people into the conversation and agrees remedies. Clients may place the manager under formal review or on a watch list.
stages.who_leads: Relationship management, escalating to the team head and senior investment staff.
stages.who_supports: Portfolio manager, risk, compliance and legal for breaches, operations for errors, consultant relations.
junior_produces: Chronology of facts for an incident
Draft holding statement and client note for compliance review
Attribution summary of what drove underperformance
Tracker of clients affected and who has been contacted
stages.client_side: Chief investment officer or pensions manager, trustee chair, consultant. They need the truth quickly, a clear account of cause and remedy, and evidence that it will not recur.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client hears bad news first from the manager, understands it, and can make a reasoned decision to stay, reduce or leave.
failure_points: The client learning of a problem from the press or its consultant
Defensive or evasive explanations
Predicting a recovery that cannot be promised
Compensation or remediation handled slowly
stages.sales_vs_rm: Stewardship under stress. A badly handled difficulty also damages origination, because consultants remember.
stages.duration_note: Unpredictable; a formal review can last several quarters.

stages.name: Additional allocations and cross-sell
stages.plain: The client considers giving the manager more money or a second, different mandate.
stages.what_happens: A need emerges from the client's changing strategy, for instance moving towards lower-risk assets, adding private markets or consolidating managers. The relationship manager recognises it, tests whether the firm has a suitable capability, and introduces the right colleagues. Even for an existing client a larger or new mandate may need a formal process. Sometimes the right conclusion is that the client should not add.
stages.who_leads: Relationship management or sales, according to the firm's coverage model.
stages.who_supports: Product specialists for the new capability, the original salesperson, pricing for relationship-level fee terms.
junior_produces: Opportunity note: the client's stated need, evidence and timing
Updated client map and exposure summary across all mandates
Fee illustration including any breakpoint effect of larger assets
Briefing for the specialist who has never met the client
stages.client_side: Investment staff and consultant. They need a proposal that reflects what the manager already knows about them and respects any limit on exposure to one firm.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client gets a relevant idea at the right time from people who understand its situation, and is not pestered with irrelevant ones.
failure_points: Pitching while an existing problem is unresolved
Proposing a product because it is a firm priority, not because it fits
Internal dispute over credit delaying the response
Ignoring the client's manager-concentration limits
stages.sales_vs_rm: The clearest overlap between origination and stewardship. Firms differ on who leads and who is credited.
stages.duration_note: Opportunistic; depends on the client's strategy cycle.

stages.name: Formal review or re-tender
stages.plain: The client deliberately tests whether the manager should keep the mandate.
stages.what_happens: Many asset owners review managers on a fixed cycle or after a trigger. The review may be a desk-based assessment by the consultant, a re-presentation to trustees, or a full re-tender against competitors. Public-sector bodies may be required to re-procure. The incumbent must show its record, how it handled problems, and why it remains the right choice for the client's current needs, which may have changed since appointment.
stages.who_leads: Relationship management, with sales where the review is a competitive tender.
stages.who_supports: Portfolio manager, RFP team, consultant relations, team head.
junior_produces: Incumbent record: performance, service statistics, incidents and how they were resolved
Summary of how the client's needs have changed since appointment
Re-tender response using the client's own history, not library text
Fee comparison and options for approval
stages.client_side: Trustees or committee, consultant, sometimes procurement. They need a fair basis for comparison and may want to see the manager challenged.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client reaffirms or changes its decision on current evidence, with the incumbent having given an honest account of its record.
failure_points: Complacency: treating the review as a formality
Defending the original mandate when the client's needs have moved on
Fee concessions offered only under threat, which damages trust
A new consultant with no history with the firm
stages.sales_vs_rm: Both. The relationship manager holds the evidence; sales brings competitive discipline.
stages.duration_note: Months; the cycle between reviews is typically several years.

stages.name: Renewal or exit
stages.plain: The mandate continues on refreshed terms, shrinks, or ends.
stages.what_happens: Renewal may bring revised guidelines, fees or reporting. Exit can be full or partial and has many causes: performance, a change in the client's strategy such as a pension scheme buying insurance for its liabilities, consolidation, a merger, or a new decision-maker's preferences. On exit the manager cooperates with the transition: providing data, selling or transferring assets in an orderly way, final reporting and fee reconciliation. How a firm behaves on the way out affects whether it is invited back.
stages.who_supports: Operations, portfolio manager, legal, the incoming transition manager where one is used.
junior_produces: Transition-out checklist and final reporting schedule
Final fee reconciliation support
Lessons-learned note recorded in the CRM
Updated contact record so the relationship can resume later
stages.client_side: Investment staff, operations, custodian, incoming manager or insurer. They need a clean, cooperative handover.
stages.good_execution_changes: The client leaves or renews with its assets and records in order and without avoidable cost.
failure_points: Obstructive or slow cooperation after notice
No record of why the client left
Treating a rational client decision as a failure to be argued with
Losing contact with people who will be decision-makers elsewhere
stages.sales_vs_rm: Stewardship to the end, then back to origination: a former client is a future prospect.
stages.duration_note: Notice periods are set by the contract; transitions take weeks to months.

tpw_variant.name: Gatekeeper research
tpw_variant.plain: A wealth manager's fund research team studies the fund before anyone is allowed to buy it.
tpw_variant.what_happens: The fund selector or research analyst screens a peer group, requests data and a questionnaire, meets the portfolio manager and scores the fund against competitors. The asset manager's salesperson supplies information in the selector's format and arranges access to the investment team.
tpw_variant.who_supports: Investment specialist, portfolio manager, marketing and data teams.
junior_produces: Selector briefing
Data in the selector's template, checked to the factsheet
Peer-group comparison
Meeting notes with open questions
tpw_variant.client_side: Fund selector or research analyst (the gatekeeper), who answers to an investment committee.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: The selector can assess the fund efficiently and accurately against alternatives.
failure_points: Data in the wrong format or late
A portfolio manager who does not answer the question asked
Pitching a fund the firm wants to sell instead of the one the selector is researching
tpw_variant.duration_note: Weeks to many months; reviews follow the selector's calendar.

tpw_variant.name: Buy-list or approved-list decision
tpw_variant.plain: The intermediary's investment committee decides whether the fund may be used.
tpw_variant.what_happens: The selector presents a recommendation to an investment committee. If approved, the fund joins a buy list, recommended list or model portfolio universe. Approval is permission to buy; it is not a purchase.
tpw_variant.who_leads: The intermediary's committee decides; sales responds to final queries.
tpw_variant.who_supports: Legal and product teams for share-class and fee terms.
junior_produces: Answers to committee follow-up questions
Share-class and fee summary
Record of the decision and its conditions in the CRM
tpw_variant.client_side: Investment committee, head of research, sometimes compliance.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: The committee decides on complete information and understands where the fund fits and where it does not.
failure_points: Assuming approval equals assets
Unclear role for the fund in portfolios
Share class or fee terms not agreed in time

tpw_variant.name: Platform availability and set-up
tpw_variant.plain: The fund must be technically available where advisers actually place trades.
tpw_variant.what_happens: The right share class is listed on the investment platforms the intermediary uses, with correct identifiers, charges and documents. Distribution agreements are completed. Data feeds to the platform and to research tools are tested.
tpw_variant.who_leads: Product and distribution operations, coordinated by the relationship manager or sales.
junior_produces: Platform availability checklist by share class
Document pack: key information, factsheet, prospectus links
Data-feed check against official figures
tpw_variant.client_side: Platform operations, the intermediary's operations and compliance staff.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: An adviser who wants to buy the fund can do so without friction, at the correct price.
failure_points: Approved fund not available on the platform advisers use
Wrong charges displayed
Missing documents blocking trades
tpw_variant.duration_note: Days to weeks, depending on the platform.

tpw_variant.name: Adviser and portfolio-manager adoption
tpw_variant.plain: The people who run client portfolios decide, one by one, whether to use the approved fund.
tpw_variant.what_happens: Advisers, discretionary portfolio managers or the team running model portfolios choose among approved funds. The asset manager supports adoption with briefings, plain-language material and access to specialists. In centrally run model portfolios one decision can move large sums; in adviser-led firms adoption is gradual.
tpw_variant.who_leads: Third-party wealth sales, with relationship management for existing holders.
junior_produces: Adviser briefing material
Event logistics and attendee follow-up
Adoption tracker by office or desk
Log of objections heard
tpw_variant.client_side: Advisers, discretionary managers, model-portfolio team; behind them, the end investor whose interests the intermediary must serve.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: Advisers understand what the fund is for and can explain it accurately to their own clients.
failure_points: Material too technical for adviser conversations
No clear reason to choose the fund over an existing holding
Coverage spread too thinly across many offices
tpw_variant.duration_note: Months to years; often never complete.

tpw_variant.name: Flows
tpw_variant.plain: Money arrives, and leaves, in many small transactions.
tpw_variant.what_happens: Subscriptions and redemptions pass through platforms daily. The manager sees aggregate flows by intermediary, with limited sight of individual end investors. Flows respond to performance, market sentiment, model-portfolio rebalancing and the intermediary's own client growth.
tpw_variant.who_leads: No single lead; sales and relationship management both monitor.
junior_produces: Weekly flow report by intermediary and fund
Explanation of unusual movements
List of approved-but-unused funds
tpw_variant.client_side: End investors through advisers and platforms.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: The manager notices early when a holder is reducing and can ask why.
failure_points: Reading gross sales without redemptions
Mistaking a model rebalance for a change of view
No follow-up on unexplained outflows

tpw_variant.name: Monitoring and ongoing due diligence
tpw_variant.plain: The gatekeeper keeps checking that the fund still deserves its place.
tpw_variant.what_happens: Selectors review held funds on a schedule and after triggers such as underperformance, a manager change or a fund growing too large. The asset manager provides updates, access to the team and prompt notice of changes. For funds reaching retail investors in the UK, the manufacturer and the distributor each carry Consumer Duty obligations, including on fair value, so value assessments and target-market information are part of the exchange.
junior_produces: Annual due-diligence update pack
Change notifications to all holders
Watch-list tracker with decision dates
Responses to value and target-market queries
tpw_variant.client_side: Fund research team, investment committee, compliance.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: The intermediary can keep using the fund with confidence, or act promptly if it should not.
failure_points: Holders learning of a manager change from the press
Slow or incomplete responses to review questions
Treating the annual review as routine

tpw_variant.name: Removal or replacement
tpw_variant.plain: The fund is taken off the list, or the intermediary itself changes.
tpw_variant.what_happens: A fund may be downgraded, put on hold or removed after poor performance, a team change, a cheaper alternative, list consolidation, or the intermediary being acquired and its lists merged. Removal can trigger rapid redemptions from model portfolios. The manager supports an orderly exit and records the reason.
tpw_variant.who_supports: Sales (for alternative funds that may fit), operations, liquidity management within the fund.
junior_produces: Record of the stated reason and the real one if different
Redemption forecast for the portfolio manager
Note on whether another capability might genuinely fit
tpw_variant.client_side: Investment committee, selectors, advisers who must explain the change to their clients.
tpw_variant.good_execution_changes: End investors are moved without avoidable cost and the intermediary remains willing to consider the manager again.
failure_points: Arguing with the decision instead of understanding it
Immediately pitching a replacement fund
No lessons recorded
